title: School Improvement Model
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart presents a school improvement model built on five assumptions: schools are complex systems, leadership is problem-solving not formula-application, expertise is required, knowledge-building is central, and leaders can influence outcomes across multiple domains (from teaching quality to organizational learning). The article distinguishes three levels of problem-solving: the individual teacher (maximising student attention, reducing cognitive load, building knowledge through responsive practice), the school leader (developing the expertise and CPD systems that support all teachers), and the multi-school leader (managing collaboration, standardisation, and a people strategy across different contexts). Hart argues that effective school improvement requires a shared language for problems and strategies -- because changing how people talk changes how they think and targets their beliefs, which is the actual lever for changing practice. The model is explicitly non-prescriptive: its value is in leaders formulating their own version for their context. The closing section offers generalisable principles, including that a model must evolve as a school improves or declines, and that individual schools in a federation require differentiated approaches based on the unique combination of circumstances each presents.
points: Schools are complex systems where nothing works everywhere and everything works somewhere; effective leadership is therefore problem-solving in context, not applying a transferable formula.
Teachers need expertise in specific domains (attention, cognitive load, ratio, scaffolding, responsive teaching) to solve the persistent problems of classroom instruction.

Leaders need expertise in curriculum, assessment, evaluation, behaviour strategy, and professional development -- but above all in designing conditions for individual, team, and organisational learning.
A school improvement model must plan for how the team talks, not just what it does, because shared language changes thinking and targets the beliefs that determine practice.
A model specific enough to address a school's needs must also be general enough to be adapted for different circumstances as context and school improvement stage evolve.
quotes: Schools are complex. There are multiple agents interacting and influencing each other in ways that vary in how predictable they are, how desirable they are and how proximal the effects are seen.

School leadership is problem solving, not applying a formula. Despite essentially doing the same work, each school has a unique context; Dylan Wilam tells us that nothing works everywhere and everything works somewhere.

Schools improve when children develop academically, socially, emotionally and much much more. At the heart of an improvement model is therefore maximising the chances that children will learn what we intend and make the most of opportunities for incidental learning in all sorts of domains too.

To make the most of these informal opportunities, it becomes vital that there is a shared language for talking about problems, priorities and strategies so a school improvement model must plan for how the team talks, not only because it allows more meaningful collaboration but because changing how we talk changes how we think and if we are to help colleagues to get better, we have to target their beliefs.

I'm not advocating that this is entirely transferable to other schools; I think that the value is in leaders formulating their model for their contexts. However, it may be of use to pull out some principles that can help guide school and executive leaders in clarifying a model that works for them.
